title: Genesis 10. The Cup Divides.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 10. The Cup Divides.
These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, Japheth.
Sons were born to them after the flood.
The Cup that held one family on one ark now pours out into dozens of peoples.
The blessing, be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, is being fulfilled.
But it is being fulfilled as division.
Every branch listed will have its own language, its own land,
its own nation.
The Cup that was one vessel is becoming many.
Japheth's sons spread to the coastlands.
Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Tiras.
Their sons extend further, Ashkenaz, Riphath, Togarmah, Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, Dodanim.
From these, the islands of the nations are divided in their lands.
Each after his language.
Each after his family.
Each in his nation.
The division is already described as a fact before the story of how it happened is told.
Ham's sons: Cush, Mizraim, Put, Canaan.
From Cush comes Nimrod.
Nimrod is the first mighty man on the earth.
A mighty hunter before the Lord.
The text pauses for him,
the only person in the chapter who receives a narrative description rather than a bare genealogy.
He began to be a mighty one.
His kingdom begins with Babel, Erech, Accad, Calneh,
in the land of Shinar.
From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir,
Calah, and Resen.
The seed of chapter eleven is already planted here.
The first kingdom on the post-flood earth begins with Babel.
The first mighty man builds the first cities.
The Cup that was divided into nations is already being gathered into an empire,
by a hunter.
The man who hunts before the Lord builds the city that will try to reach heaven in the next chapter.
Mizraim fathers the peoples of Egypt.
Canaan fathers Sidon, his firstborn, Heth, the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,
the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, the Hamathites.
The Canaanite clans spread abroad.
Their border runs from Sidon toward Gerar, toward Gaza, toward Sodom, Gomorrah,
Admah, and Zeboiim, to Lasha.
The names of cities that do not yet exist as places of judgment are already named as boundaries.
Sodom and Gomorrah appear on a map before they appear in a story.
Then the line of Shem, the elder brother of Japheth,
the father of all the children of Eber.
Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram.
Arpachshad fathers Shelah.
Shelah fathers Eber.
To Eber are born two sons.
One is named Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided.
His brother is Joktan.
In his days the earth was divided.
The division that chapter eleven will describe as a divine act is already noted here,
in a name, in a genealogy.
Peleg means division.
The Cup divided before the story of division is told.
What chapter eleven will show as a tower and a confusion of languages is already witnessed in chapter ten as a fact:
the nations separated, each with its own language, in its own land,
among its own people.
These are the families of the sons of Noah,
according to their generations, in their nations.
From these the nations were divided on the earth after the flood.
The chapter is a map.
Not of geography only,
but of how the one family that survived the flood became the many families that fill the earth.
The covenant-carrying line narrows, Shem's descendants run through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg,
toward a man who has not yet been named.
The Cup pours out into every nation.
But inside the pouring,
one line carries a thread that has not yet found its end.
